title: Building effective agents
date: 19 December 2024; live page edited since, undated
scope: Full live article text with both appendices; diagrams not inspected. Quotes come from the live page, which now names later models and SDKs.
role: Start with the simplest design and add complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes; workflows versus agents; tool definitions engineered like prompts; stopping conditions such as an iteration cap; testing in sandboxed environments.
note: Vendor guidance from Anthropic's customer work, with no quantitative evidence. Stopping conditions are described as common practice, not a requirement; the step cap, its value and what happens at the cap are Senoni choices.

title: Writing effective tools for agents — with agents
scope: Full article text; the example responses and evaluation charts are images and were not read.
role: A few well-chosen tools rather than wrapped endpoints; distinct names and namespacing; high-signal, token-efficient responses with pagination or truncation; actionable error messages; evaluating tools on realistic tasks.
note: Vendor guidance based on Anthropic's internal tools, not an independent study; it says naming and response formats should be settled by your own evaluations. Enums over free text and the allowlist inside the tool are Senoni choices.

title: Effective context engineering for AI agents
scope: Full article text; figures not inspected and linked studies not followed.
role: Context engineering as curating the tokens in the window; context as a finite resource with diminishing returns; just-in-time retrieval, compaction, structured note-taking and sub-agents.
note: Vendor guidance illustrated with Anthropic products. It presents context engineering as the progression of prompt engineering rather than a separate practice; its context-rot claim refers to studies the text doesn't cite.

title: The New Skill in AI is Not Prompting, It's Context Engineering
scope: Full text of the short post; linked sources not followed.
role: A definition of context as everything the model sees before it responds.
note: A short opinion piece with no data. Cite it for the definition only: it doesn't cover compaction, note-taking or sub-agents (FD03a does).

title: A practical guide to building agents
date: 2025 (PDF metadata 7 April 2025; an HTML version is dated 15 January 2026)
scope: Full text of the 34-page PDF, extracted; key passages checked against the HTML version. Code samples and diagrams not read.
role: Maximise a single agent before adding agents; layered guardrails; rating each tool low, medium or high by read or write access, reversibility, permissions and financial impact; human intervention for high-risk actions and when failure thresholds are exceeded.
note: Vendor guidance from unspecified customer deployments, with no data or thresholds. The pack's autonomy table adapts these risk factors; adding verifiability as a factor is Senoni's choice.

title: Best practices for Claude Code
scope: Full current page, and the opening of the hooks guide (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide).
role: Explore, plan, then code, reviewing the plan before implementation; a CLAUDE.md for commands, conventions and workflow; permission allowlists; hooks as deterministic controls, unlike advisory instructions.
note: Undated product documentation that changes often. It advises skipping the plan for a change you can describe in one sentence. Prompt- and agent-based hooks call a model and are not deterministic in the same sense.

title: Claude Code: Best practices for agentic coding
scope: Archived copy of 30 June 2025: header, author line and the workflow sections. The original address now redirects to FD05a.
role: Test-first with a coding agent: write tests, run them and confirm they fail, then implement until they pass.
note: Superseded by FD05a, which no longer includes the confirm-they-fail step; cite this archived version for that step only.

title: AGENTS.md
scope: Full single-page site, including the FAQ.
role: AGENTS.md as a predictable place for agent instructions; nested files in subprojects, the closest taking precedence.
note: The format's own page, not a study. Precedence depends on each agent's implementation, which the page doesn't verify; adoption figures are self-reported.

title: Your AI Product Needs Evals
scope: Full current post, compared with an archived copy of 1 April 2024 to see what was added later.
role: Evaluation at the centre of iteration; assertions as unit tests; looking at traces; tracking agreement between an LLM judge and human judgement.
note: A practitioner essay built on one case study. A later, undated box warns that raw agreement misleads with imbalanced classes and recommends precision and recall. The post doesn't mention kappa (FD10a).

title: Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations
scope: Full v1 text and appendices; wording and page numbers checked in the PDF.
role: Report standard errors with eval scores; cluster them when questions are related; compare models with paired differences; resample answers to reduce variance; size an eval with power analysis.
note: A single-author preprint whose worked examples use fictional numbers (Tables 1 and 2 disagree on one score). Its 95% interval is the mean plus or minus 1.96 standard errors, which for a pass rate is the Wald interval FD22b advises against at small n; the pack uses Wilson intervals there.

title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
date: 2023 (NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks; arXiv v4 24 December 2023)
scope: Abstract to section 4.2 with Tables 1–6 in the arXiv v4 HTML; quotes and pages checked in the PDF. Sections 4.3–6 and the appendices not read.
role: LLM judges show position and verbosity bias; strong judges agree with people about as often as people agree with each other; a reference answer cut grading failures on math questions.
note: Self-enhancement bias is listed in the abstract, but section 3.3 says the study couldn't establish it. Agreement is raw, not chance-corrected. The reference-guided result rests on 10 math questions, and the judges are 2023 models.

title: A Coefficient of Agreement for Nominal Scales
scope: Publisher record and reference list only; the article is paywalled. The definition was checked in Cohen's own 1986 Citation Classic commentary (Current Contents, 20 January 1986, in Eugene Garfield's archive) and in FD10b.
role: Kappa: agreement between two raters corrected for the agreement expected by chance.
note: The 1960 text was not read. Cohen's 1986 commentary gives the motivating case: two raters who each label 10% of cases at random agree 82% of the time, yet kappa is 0.

title: sklearn.metrics.cohen_kappa_score
scope: Whole API page: definition, parameters, return value, references and example.
role: The working definition of kappa, with expected agreement taken from each rater's own label distribution, citing FD10a.
note: Secondary documentation, not the original paper. The stable address follows each release; pin the version when citing.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
scope: Full arXiv HTML text with appendices, and the abstract page's metadata.
role: Retrieval as a non-parametric memory beside the generator; updating knowledge by swapping the index without retraining.
note: The hot-swap evidence is one small test (82 world leaders, a 2016 index against a 2018 one). RAG itself is fine-tuned end to end; swapping works because the document encoder and index stay frozen.

title: The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond
publisher: Foundations and Trends in Information Retrieval 3(4):333–389, now publishers
scope: Title page, abstract and sections 3.4.2–3.5.1 (pp. 356–361) of the author-hosted PDF on Stephen Robertson's City, University of London page; the publisher's copy is paywalled.
role: BM25's term-frequency saturation (k1) and document-length normalisation (b), with starting ranges for both.
note: The ranges are rules of thumb, 0.5 < b < 0.8 and 1.2 < k1 < 2, and the best values depend on the documents and queries. The source does not give b = 0.75 as a default.

title: How we built our multi-agent research system
scope: Full post, including the appendix.
role: Multi-agent systems use about 15 times the tokens of chat; they suit breadth-first, parallel work and fit poorly where agents share context or depend on each other; evaluate early with small samples, a rubric judge and people; errors compound in stateful agents, so resume rather than restart.
note: A vendor write-up of its own product, with internal figures and no published method; the conclusions are scoped to research tasks.

title: Don’t Build Multi-Agents
scope: Full post.
role: Share full context and traces; actions carry implicit decisions, so conflicting decisions give bad results; a single-threaded agent is the simple default.
note: An opinion essay from a vendor, with illustrative examples and no data, dated to 2025 capabilities. It allows sub-agents that only answer well-defined questions, and agrees with FD13 on the shared-context constraint despite the opposite headline.

title: The lethal trifecta for AI agents: private data, untrusted content, and external communication
scope: Full post.
role: The three ingredients and why combining them lets an attacker steal data; why guardrails that claim to catch 95% of attacks are not enough.
note: A short opinion post. Its advice to avoid the combination is addressed mainly to users who mix tools; 'remove a leg' is our phrasing, not Willison's. For developers it points to FD17.

title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025
scope: The list page, and the full LLM01, LLM02 and LLM06 pages; the PDF and the other seven entries not read.
role: The ten 2025 risk names and IDs; prevention lists for prompt injection (LLM01), sensitive information disclosure (LLM02) and excessive agency (LLM06).
note: LLM01 itself says it is unclear whether fool-proof prevention exists. LLM02 frames sanitisation mainly around training data and never says minimisation (FD24a does). The LLM06 page still uses the 2023 name Insecure Output Handling.

title: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections
scope: Abstract, sections 1–3, the introduction to section 4 and 4.1, section 5 and Appendix A in the arXiv HTML; case studies 4.2–4.10 searched, not read in full.
role: Six patterns that isolate untrusted data from the agent's control flow (action-selector, plan-then-execute, LLM map-reduce, dual LLM, code-then-execute, context-minimisation), and the principle that untrusted input must not be able to trigger consequential actions. The action-selector pattern prevents any feedback from the actions back into the agent (section 3.1, re-read 21 October 2026).
note: A preprint. The authors say the patterns trade utility for security and that general-purpose agents can't yet be secured. Author order is alphabetical, so the short citation says nothing about who led the work.

title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
scope: Executive summary, the end of section 4, all of section 5 (the core and Tables 1–4) and section 6 in the PDF; part 1 sections 1–3 and the appendices not read in detail.
role: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage; an initial go/no-go decision once context, purpose, benefits and costs are mapped (section 5.2 and MAP 3); mechanisms to supersede, disengage or deactivate a system (MANAGE 2.4).
note: A voluntary US framework with no legal force. NIST says version 1.0 is being revised, so the wording may change.

title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, NIST AI 600-1
publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
scope: Sections 1–2 (the twelve risks) and selected section 3 actions (GV-1.3, GV-1.7, MP-1.1, MS-2.7, MS-4.2, MG-2.4); the rest of section 3 and the appendices not read.
role: Generative AI risks, including data privacy and information security, with prompt injection under the latter; minimum thresholds in deployment go/no-go decisions (GV-1.3-002); criteria for deactivation (MG-2.4-004); red-teaming for prompt injection (MS-2.7-007).
note: A voluntary companion profile; its suggested actions cover only some subcategories. Printed page numbers are four less than the PDF's.

title: Probable Inference, the Law of Succession, and Statistical Inference
publisher: Journal of the American Statistical Association 22(158):209–212
scope: Bibliographic record only; the publisher's and JSTOR's copies were not reachable. The attribution of the score interval was checked in FD22b.
role: Origin of the score interval for a binomial proportion, used for pass rates and miss rates.
note: Wilson's text was not read; the attribution rests on FD22b, which says the interval seems to have been introduced here.

title: Interval Estimation for a Binomial Proportion
publisher: Statistical Science 16(2):101–133, Institute of Mathematical Statistics
scope: Abstract, section 1, passages of sections 3.1.1 and 3.2, and section 5, in the PDF on T. Tony Cai's site; the discussion and rejoinder not read.
role: The standard (Wald) interval's coverage can be poor even at large n; for n of 40 or less, use the Wilson or Jeffreys interval.
note: About two-sided intervals for one proportion. For n above 40 the authors prefer Agresti–Coull for its simplicity; using Wilson throughout is Senoni's choice.

title: A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = λW
scope: Publisher record and abstract; the first and last pages viewed in a course-reading copy, the proof pages not read closely.
role: L = λW: the average number in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time in it.
note: A proof under stationarity; FD23b covers practice and finite windows. No open copy exists, so cite the DOI.

title: Little's Law as Viewed on Its 50th Anniversary
scope: Sections 1–3.1 (pp. 536–541) of the free copy on INFORMS's own site, and targeted passages of the rest.
role: Little's law in practice, and that over a finite window starting and ending empty it holds exactly, without stationarity.
note: A retrospective essay, not a new study.

title: Guidance on AI and data protection

Read in full on 21 October 2026: the ICO's page on data protection officers in its guide to accountability and governance (https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/accountability-and-governance/guide-to-accountability-and-governance/data-protection-officers/).
role: Identify the minimum personal data the purpose needs; AI adds security complexity; AI processing usually needs a data protection impact assessment; a data protection officer informs, advises and monitors, while compliance stays the controller's or processor's responsibility.

title: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs
scope: Full article text; diagrams not read.

note: Amazon's own practice. The response is semantically equivalent, not identical, and identifiers are kept for a limited time; recording the identifier and the mutation must be one atomic operation.
